summary: The SR-71 Blackbird was an American spy plane that flew higher and faster than any other jet aircraft with a pilot, at more than three times the speed of sound. It still holds the world speed record for an air-breathing crewed aircraft, set in 1976.
funFacts: About 85 per cent of its structure was made of titanium, some of it secretly bought from the Soviet Union through fake companies.
Its fuel tanks could not be sealed well enough to cope with the huge temperature changes in flight, so it leaked fuel on the ground before take-off.
In 1974 it flew from New York to London in 1 hour, 54 minutes and 56 seconds.
If a missile was launched at it, the standard plan was simply to speed up and outrun it.
spotterTips: A long, flat, all-black jet with sharp ridges called chines along its sides, two huge engines in the middle of the wings and two inward-leaning tail fins.

name: Cessna 172 Skyhawk
summary: The Cessna 172 is a small four-seat aeroplane that thousands of pilots learn to fly in. More 172s have been built than any other aircraft in history, and it has been in production on and off since 1956.
funFacts: In 1958 and 1959 two pilots kept a Cessna 172 in the air for 64 days, 22 hours and 19 minutes without landing, refuelling in flight. It was a world record for flight endurance.
During that record flight they covered an estimated 240,000 km, more than six times around the Earth at the equator.
In 1987 a German teenager named Mathias Rust flew a rented Cessna 172 from Finland all the way to Moscow and landed near Red Square without being stopped.
The 172 was developed from the Cessna 170 but swapped the tail wheel for a nose wheel, which made it much easier to land.
spotterTips: Look for a high wing held up by a single strut on each side, a nose wheel, and a single propeller. It looks very similar to other Cessnas, but the 172 has four seats and a fairly short, straight tail with a sloping fin.

melbourne.where: Moorabbin Airport is the busiest place to see them, with flight schools flying circuits all day. They are also common at Lilydale, Tyabb and other country airfields around Victoria.
melbourne.operators: Flight schools and aero clubs, plus private owners

name: Piper PA-28 Cherokee
role: Two to four-seat training and touring aeroplane
summary: The Piper Cherokee is a family of small, all-metal aeroplanes used for flight training and private flying. It is the main rival to the Cessna 172 and is one of the most produced aircraft ever, with versions like the Warrior and Archer still being built today.
funFacts: The PA-28 is the fourth most produced aircraft in history.
It has only one door, on the right side, so everyone climbs in by stepping up onto the wing.
Piper has fitted Cherokee family aircraft with engines from 140 to 300 horsepower, and some versions even have retractable landing gear.
Newer Archer DX and DLX models run on a diesel engine instead of normal aviation petrol.
spotterTips: The Cherokee has a low wing (underneath the cabin), one propeller and a nose wheel. If it looks like a Cessna 172 turned upside down with the wing on the bottom, it is probably a Piper.

melbourne.where: Common at Moorabbin Airport and at Victorian airfields such as Lilydale and Tyabb.
melbourne.operators: Flight schools, aero clubs and private owners

photo.file: G-AVRZ Piper PA-28-180 Cherokee C at Northrepps.jpg

name: Cirrus SR22
role: Four or five-seat fast touring aeroplane
summary: The Cirrus SR22 is a sleek, fast four-seater made from composite materials instead of metal. It has been the world's best-selling small private aeroplane every year since 2003, and it carries a parachute big enough to lower the whole aeroplane to the ground.
funFacts: If something goes badly wrong, the pilot can pull a handle that fires a rocket to pull out a giant parachute and float the entire aeroplane down.
By September 2018 the parachute had been used 79 times, with 163 people surviving.
It was the first light aircraft to come with a full glass cockpit, meaning screens instead of round dials.
Cirrus skipped the name G4 and went straight from G3 to G5, because the number four is considered unlucky in some cultures.
spotterTips: A low wing, one propeller, a smooth shiny composite body and a long, slender wing. Look for the curved cabin roof and the parachute cover behind the rear window.

melbourne.where: Seen at Moorabbin Airport and Essendon Fields, and at country airfields around Victoria.
melbourne.operators: Private owners and some flight schools

name: Diamond DA40 Diamond Star
summary: The DA40 is a modern four-seat training aeroplane from Austria built mostly from composite materials. Its long glider-like wings and good safety record make it popular with schools that train future airline pilots.
funFacts: DA40s are built in two countries: Austria and Canada.
Some versions run on diesel or jet fuel instead of aviation petrol.
The very first prototype flew with a Rotax engine, the same kind of engine family used in many small sport aircraft.
A study in 2011 found the DA40 had one of the best safety records of any light aircraft.
spotterTips: Low wing with a T-shaped tail (the horizontal tail sits on top of the fin) and a big bubble canopy. The wings are long and thin like a glider's.

melbourne.where: Flight training airfields around Melbourne, including Moorabbin.
melbourne.operators: Flight schools, especially those training airline pilots

name: Piper J-3 Cub
role: Two-seat light trainer and sport aeroplane
numberBuilt: About 20,000 (19,888 in the US plus 150 in Canada)
summary: The Piper Cub is a simple, slow, lightweight aeroplane from the late 1930s that taught a huge number of people to fly. It was so cheap and popular it has been compared to the Ford Model T car, and many are still flying today.
funFacts: When flown solo, the pilot sits in the back seat so the aeroplane stays balanced.
A Cub flying over Hawaii during the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941 was shot down, making it the first American aeroplane shot down in World War II. The student pilot parachuted to safety.
In World War II an army version called the L-4 Grasshopper spotted for artillery, and one called Rosie the Rocketer was even fitted with bazookas.
Its bright yellow paint became so famous it is known as Cub Yellow.
spotterTips: A bright yellow high-wing aeroplane with struts, a tail wheel instead of a nose wheel, and two seats one behind the other. The engine cylinders often poke out of the nose.

name: Pilatus PC-12
role: Single-engine turboprop for business, cargo and air ambulance work
engines: 1 × Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6A-67P turboprop (1,200 shp)
summary: The PC-12 is a Swiss single-engine turboprop that can carry people, cargo or stretcher patients a long way at high altitude. The Royal Flying Doctor Service was its first customer and is still one of its biggest users.
funFacts: The Royal Flying Doctor Service in Australia was the launch customer for the PC-12.
Its cabin can be set up as an air ambulance carrying two stretchers and three medical staff.
The interior was designed with help from BMW's design team.
It has a large rear cargo door, so it can carry big items that would never fit through a normal aeroplane door.
spotterTips: One turboprop engine in the nose, a low wing with small upturned winglets, and a tall T-tail. It is bigger than most single-engine aeroplanes.

melbourne.where: Royal Flying Doctor Service PC-12s fly all over Australia and can visit Melbourne airports. Business and charter PC-12s use Essendon Fields and Moorabbin.
melbourne.operators: Royal Flying Doctor Service, charter companies and private owners

photo.file: Royal Flying Doctor Service of Australia (VH-OWR) Pilatus PC-12 NG at Esperance Airport.jpg

name: Beechcraft King Air
engines: 2 × Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6A-135A turboprops (550 shp each)
summary: The King Air is a twin-engine turboprop family used as a business aircraft, air ambulance and military transport. It was the first aircraft of its kind and outsold all of its turboprop rivals combined.
funFacts: A King Air was used by US President Lyndon Johnson, and when he was on board it used the call sign Air Force One.
The King Air line was built continuously from 1964 to 2021.
Bigger versions with a T-tail were sold as Super King Airs. They are the ones you usually see on air ambulance work in Australia.
The US Army flew a version called the U-21 Ute.
spotterTips: Two turboprop engines on a low wing and a round-nosed cabin with oval windows. The smaller 90 series has a normal tail, while the bigger 200, 260, 350 and 360 models have a T-tail.

melbourne.where: Ambulance Victoria's fixed-wing air ambulances, King Air 260 and 360 models, are based at Essendon Airport and fly patients across Victoria. Other King Airs visit Essendon Fields and Moorabbin.
melbourne.operators: Ambulance Victoria (aircraft operated by Toll Aviation), charter companies and businesses

photo.file: Royal Flying Doctor Service (VH-AMR) Beechcraft B200C King Air (2).jpg

name: Cessna 208 Caravan
engines: 1 × Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6A-114A turboprop (675 shp)
summary: The Caravan is a tough single-engine turboprop that works almost anywhere: carrying cargo, small groups of passengers, skydivers or supplies to remote places. It can land on wheels, floats or skis.
funFacts: A version with no cabin windows, the Cargomaster, was built specially for FedEx to carry parcels.
By 2022, Caravans had flown a combined 24 million hours.
Skydiving versions can be fitted with a roller door at the back so jumpers can leap straight out.
The Caravan Amphibian has floats with wheels built in, so it can land on water or a runway.
spotterTips: A big high-wing aeroplane with struts, one turboprop engine in a long nose, and fixed landing gear. Many carry a cargo pod under the belly.

melbourne.where: Look for them at skydiving centres and regional airfields around Victoria, and at Moorabbin and Essendon on charter or cargo work.
melbourne.operators: Skydiving operators, charter and freight companies

photo.file: Iraqi Air Force Cessna 208 Caravan training mission.jpg

name: de Havilland Canada DHC-2 Beaver
role: Rugged bush plane for short and rough airstrips
engines: 1 × Pratt & Whitney R-985 Wasp Junior radial engine (450 hp)
summary: The Beaver is a famous Canadian bush plane built to take off and land in very short spaces, often on floats from lakes. It became a Canadian icon for flying people and supplies into remote wilderness.
funFacts: Its oil filler is inside the cockpit, so the pilot can top up the oil while flying.
When engineers worried it would be slow, a bush pilot replied that it only had to be faster than a dog sled.
In 1987 it was named one of Canada's top ten engineering achievements of the 20th century.
An electric Beaver, the Harbour Air e-Beaver, has been flown in Canada as a test of battery-powered seaplanes.
spotterTips: A chunky high-wing aeroplane with struts and a big round radial engine at the front. It is very often seen on floats.

photo.file: VH-IDO De Havilland Canada DHC-2 Beaver Mk1 Airwaves Gold Coast (8402101541).jpg

name: Gulfstream G650
summary: The G650 is a large, very fast private jet that can fly nonstop between distant continents. When it arrived it was Gulfstream's biggest and fastest jet, and it later led to the even longer G700 and G800.
funFacts: During testing a G650 reached Mach 0.995, just under the speed of sound, in a dive.
The G650 project won the Collier Trophy, one of America's top aviation awards, in 2014.
It can cruise at up to 15,500 m, well above most airliners.
The G650ER version carries extra fuel and once flew nonstop from Hong Kong to New Jersey in the United States.
spotterTips: A big, sleek jet with two engines mounted on the rear of the body, a T-tail and large oval windows. The wings are swept and have upturned winglets.

melbourne.where: Essendon Fields is the main business jet airport in Melbourne. Large private jets also use Melbourne Airport and Avalon.
melbourne.operators: Private owners, companies and charter operators

name: Bombardier Global 7500
summary: The Global 7500 is one of the largest and longest-range private jets ever built. Its cabin is split into four separate rooms, and it can fly nonstop between cities on opposite sides of the world.
funFacts: In 2019 a Global 7500 flew nonstop from Sydney to Detroit in the United States, about 15,230 km, a record for a purpose-built business jet.
It was the first business jet designed with a four-zone cabin, which can include a bedroom.
By March 2025 it had set 100 officially recognised speed records.
A test aircraft from the same family briefly went faster than the speed of sound, reaching Mach 1.015, in 2021.
spotterTips: A very long jet with two engines on the rear of the body, a T-tail and lots of large windows. It looks like a small airliner but with fewer, bigger windows.

melbourne.where: Essendon Fields is the main place to see private jets in Melbourne. Very large private jets also use Melbourne Airport and Avalon.
melbourne.operators: Private owners, companies and charter operators

name: Cessna Citation CJ4
numberBuilt: More than 400 CJ4s (over 2,000 of the whole CitationJet family by 2017)
summary: The CJ4 is the biggest member of Cessna's CitationJet family of small business jets. Like the others it can be flown by a single pilot, which makes it popular with owners who fly themselves. The family first flew in 1991.
funFacts: The CitationJet family is certified to be flown by just one pilot, which is unusual for a jet.
The CJ4 is the only member of the family with swept-back wings. The smaller ones have straight wings.
The CitationJet's wing was developed with help from NASA and Boeing.
The 400th CJ4 was delivered in April 2023.
spotterTips: A small jet with two engines mounted on the rear of the body and a T-tail. The CJ4 has slightly swept wings, while the smaller CJs have straight wings.

melbourne.where: Essendon Fields and Moorabbin are the best places to see small business jets around Melbourne.
melbourne.operators: Private owners, companies and charter operators

name: Extra EA-300
specsVariant: EA-330LT (later development, the only full specifications in the source)
summary: The Extra 300 is a German aerobatic aeroplane built to loop, roll and tumble through the sky in top-level competitions and airshows. It was designed by German aerobatic pilot Walter Extra.
funFacts: It is built to handle plus or minus 10 g with one person on board, meaning forces ten times normal gravity.
Its wing has the same shape on top and bottom, so it flies just as well upside down as the right way up.
The Extra 300L can roll at 400 degrees per second, more than a full turn in under a second.
An electric version, the Extra 330LE, set speed records in 2017 with a Siemens electric motor.
spotterTips: A small, colourful aeroplane with a tail wheel, a big propeller and a bubble canopy. The wing sits low (300L) or in the middle of the body (original 300), and it often trails smoke at airshows.

melbourne.where: Aerobatic displays at the Australian International Airshow at Avalon and at smaller airshows and fly-ins around Victoria.
melbourne.operators: Airshow pilots, aerobatic schools and private owners

name: Air Tractor AT-802 Fireboss
role: Single-engine water bomber and crop sprayer
engines: 1 × Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6A-67AG turboprop (1,350 shp)
summary: The AT-802 is a big single-engine aeroplane built to carry a huge tank of water, fire retardant or farm chemicals. The Fire Boss version has floats so it can skim across a lake, scoop up water and fly straight back to the fire.
funFacts: Its hopper holds about 3,100 litres, which is roughly the water in 20 full bathtubs.
The Fire Boss can scoop up about 3,200 litres of water from a lake or dam in around 14 seconds without stopping.
Fire Boss floats have wheels in them, so the aeroplane can land on a runway or on water.
An armoured military version, the AT-802U, has been ordered by US Special Operations Command.
spotterTips: A big single-engine aeroplane with a long nose, low wing, tail wheel and a cockpit set high up. Fire Boss versions sit on two large floats.

melbourne.where: During the Victorian bushfire season, Fire Boss and wheeled AT-802 water bombers are contracted to fight fires and are based at airfields around the state.
melbourne.operators: Forest Fire Management Victoria, the Country Fire Authority and Fire Rescue Victoria (through contracted aerial firefighting companies)

name: Canadair CL-415 Super Scooper
manufacturer: Canadair, later Bombardier and De Havilland Canada
passengers: None when firefighting (up to 18 paratroopers in other roles)
summary: The CL-415 is a flying boat designed from the start to fight fires. It skims across a lake or the sea, scoops thousands of litres of water into its belly, and drops it on the fire without ever landing.
funFacts: It scoops about 6,137 litres of water in a 12 second run across the water at about 130 km/h.
It can mix foam into the water to make it better at putting out fires.
Its older relative, the CL-215, was the first aircraft ever designed specifically as a water bomber.
A modernised version, the DHC-515, is now being built in Calgary, Canada.
spotterTips: A boat-shaped body, a high straight wing with two turboprop engines, small floats under the wingtips, and usually bright yellow and red paint.

name: Bell X-1
engines: 1 × Reaction Motors XLR11 four-chamber rocket engine
summary: The Bell X-1 was the first crewed aeroplane to fly faster than the speed of sound. On 14 October 1947, Chuck Yeager flew it to Mach 1.06 over the Mojave Desert in California.
funFacts: Its shape was copied from a .50 calibre machine gun bullet, because bullets were known to stay stable at supersonic speed.
It was carried up under a B-29 bomber and dropped in mid-air before lighting its rocket.
Yeager named his X-1 Glamorous Glennis after his wife.
The original X-1 now hangs in the National Air and Space Museum in Washington DC, painted bright orange.
spotterTips: A short, bullet-shaped orange rocket plane with thin straight wings and a cockpit blended into the nose.

name: North American X-15
summary: The X-15 was a rocket plane that flew so fast and so high in the 1960s that some of its pilots earned astronaut wings. It still holds the record as the fastest crewed, powered aeroplane ever flown.
funFacts: It reached about 7,274 km/h, more than six times the speed of sound.
Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the Moon, was one of its test pilots.
Pilot Joe Walker flew it above 100 km, the internationally recognised edge of space, in 1963.
It was dropped from under the wing of a B-52 bomber, and its thick wedge-shaped tail made as much drag as a whole fighter jet at low speed.
spotterTips: A long, black, dart-shaped rocket plane with tiny stubby wings and a big wedge-shaped tail above and below the body.

name: Lockheed Martin X-59 Quesst
role: Quiet supersonic research aeroplane for NASA
summary: The X-59 is a NASA research jet designed to fly faster than sound while making only a soft thump instead of a loud sonic boom. If it works, it could help bring back supersonic passenger flights over land.
funFacts: Its nose is so long that the pilot cannot see straight ahead, so a 4K camera and a screen show the view in front.
Its cockpit, ejection seat and canopy came from a T-38 jet trainer, and its landing gear from an F-16.
It is designed to make a thump about as loud as a car door closing, rather than a boom.
It first went supersonic in June 2026 and reached Mach 1.4 a week later.
spotterTips: An extremely long, needle-thin nose, small wings set far back, and a single engine on top of the body behind the cockpit.

photo.artist: NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center / Lori Losey
photo.file: NASA’s X-59 in Flight Above the Mojave Desert (AFRC2025-0168-038).jpg

name: Boom XB-1
summary: The XB-1 was a small test jet built by the company Boom to try out ideas for a future supersonic airliner called Overture. In January 2025 it became the first privately developed jet to fly faster than the speed of sound.
funFacts: It went supersonic three times on its first supersonic flight, on 28 January 2025, reaching Mach 1.1.
Boom said its supersonic flights did not create a sonic boom that could be heard on the ground.
It is made mostly from carbon fibre, with titanium and stainless steel in the hottest parts.
After its last flight in February 2025 it was retired to go on display at Boom's headquarters in Colorado.
spotterTips: A slim, pointy jet with a delta-shaped wing and three engines: two under the wings and one in the tail.

photo.file: Boom XB-1 mockup Wings Over the Rockies 2023.jpg

name: Solar Impulse 2
engines: 4 × electric motors (17.4 hp each) powered by solar cells and batteries
summary: Solar Impulse 2 was an aeroplane powered only by sunlight. In 2015 and 2016 it flew all the way around the world without using any fuel, storing solar energy in batteries so it could keep flying through the night.
funFacts: Its wingspan of 71.9 m is wider than a Boeing 747, yet it weighed only about as much as a large car.
One leg, from Japan to Hawaii, lasted almost 118 hours (nearly five days), a record for solar-powered flight.
The round-the-world trip took 506 days, including a long stop to repair overheated batteries.
It was later sold and turned into an uncrewed drone, and it crashed into the Gulf of Mexico in May 2026 after more than 192 hours of nonstop flight.
spotterTips: An enormously long, thin wing covered in dark solar cells, with four small propellers and a tiny cockpit pod in the middle.

name: Stratolaunch Roc
role: Giant carrier aircraft for launching hypersonic test vehicles
summary: The Stratolaunch Roc has the longest wingspan of any aeroplane ever flown, at about 117 m. It has two bodies joined by one huge wing and carries rocket-powered test vehicles high into the sky before dropping them.
funFacts: Its wingspan is longer than an American football field.
It rolls on 28 wheels and uses engines, cockpit parts and other systems taken from Boeing 747 airliners.
Only the right-hand body has crew in it. The left-hand cockpit is empty.
It is named after the Roc, a mythical bird said to be big enough to carry an elephant.
spotterTips: Two separate fuselages side by side, joined by one enormously long wing with six jet engines. Nothing else looks like it.

name: Rutan Voyager
engines: 2 × Teledyne Continental piston engines (one pulling at the front, one pushing at the back)
summary: Voyager was the first aeroplane to fly all the way around the world without stopping or refuelling. Dick Rutan and Jeana Yeager flew it in December 1986 in just over nine days.
funFacts: The idea was first sketched on the back of a napkin over lunch.
It was so full of fuel at take-off that the wingtips scraped the runway and broke off pieces of the wing.
It landed with only about 1.5 percent of its fuel left.
The empty airframe weighed only about 426 kg, but fully fuelled the aeroplane weighed about 4,400 kg.
spotterTips: A very long, bendy wing, a small front wing (canard) on the nose, two tail booms and propellers at both the front and back of the central pod.

photo.artist: NASA Armstrong Flight Research Center / Thomas Harrop
photo.file: Voyager aircraft return from non-stop trip around the world (EC87-0029-02).jpg

name: Hughes H-4 Hercules (Spruce Goose)
role: Giant wooden flying boat transport prototype
engines: 8 × Pratt & Whitney R-4360 Wasp Major radial engines (3,000 hp each)
passengers: Designed for up to 750 troops (never carried)
summary: The Spruce Goose is a gigantic wooden flying boat built by Howard Hughes during World War II to carry troops and tanks across the Atlantic. It flew only once, for less than a minute, and is now in a museum in Oregon, USA.
funFacts: Despite its nickname, it is made almost entirely of birch wood, not spruce, because metal was being saved for the war.
Its only flight lasted 26 seconds at about 21 m above the water, covering about 1.6 km.
It was designed to carry 750 soldiers or two Sherman tanks.
It is the largest seaplane ever built, and its wingspan was the longest of any aeroplane until the Stratolaunch Roc flew in 2019.
spotterTips: An enormous flying boat with a boat-shaped hull, a very long high wing carrying eight propeller engines, and floats under the wings.

name: Boeing MQ-28 Ghost Bat
role: Uncrewed combat aircraft that flies alongside crewed jets
numberBuilt: At least 8 Block 1 prototypes, with Block 2 aircraft in production
crew: None (uncrewed, controlled from the ground or from another aircraft)
summary: The Ghost Bat is a stealthy robot jet designed and built in Australia to fly as a loyal wingman next to crewed aircraft like the F-35, Super Hornet and E-7 Wedgetail. It is the first combat aircraft designed and developed in Australia in more than 50 years.
funFacts: It is named after the ghost bat, an Australian native bat that hunts in groups.
Its whole nose can be swapped for a different one, carrying different equipment for each mission.
In December 2025 a Ghost Bat fired an AIM-120 missile and destroyed a target drone, reportedly the first time an uncrewed aircraft had fired that missile.
Its wing is the largest single piece of resin-infused composite Boeing has ever made.
spotterTips: A small, smooth, angular jet with no cockpit windows, a pointed nose, and two tail fins angled outwards in a V shape.

melbourne.where: Ghost Bats are designed and built by Boeing Australia in Melbourne, though flight testing happens far away at Woomera in South Australia. Your best chance to see one is on display at the Australian International Airshow at Avalon.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (in testing with Boeing Australia)

photo.artist: U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Adrien Tran
photo.file: MQ-28 Ghost Bat prepares to conduct a taxi test during Exercise Valiant Shield 2026 at Rota.jpg

name: Airbus A340
summary: The A340 is a long-range Airbus wide-body jet with four engines, built for flying very long distances over oceans. It shares its wing and much of its body with the twin-engine A330, but its four engines let it fly routes that twin jets were not allowed to fly in the 1990s.
funFacts: Airbus gave the A340 four engines partly so it could avoid the special rules that limited how far twin-engine jets could fly from an airport.
A Singapore Airlines A340-500 once flew what was then the longest scheduled non-stop flight in the world, about 15,344 km.
The stretched A340-600 is more than 75 metres long, longer than the A340-300 by almost 12 metres.
Four engines use a lot of fuel, which is why airlines replaced most A340s with newer twin-engine jets like the A350 and 787.
spotterTips: Count the engines. The A340 has four slim engines under a long wing, while the very similar A330 has only two. Look also for an extra set of main wheels under the middle of the belly.

photo.file: Frankfurt Airport Lufthansa Airbus A340-313 D-AIGY (DSC02566).jpg

name: Boeing 767
role: Medium to long-range wide-body airliner, freighter and military tanker
status: In service (freighter and military tanker versions still being built)
engines: 2 × Pratt & Whitney PW4060 turbofans (GE CF6 and Rolls-Royce RB211 engines were also offered)
passengers: 261 in two classes, up to 290 in one class
summary: The 767 is a twin-aisle Boeing jet that is smaller than a 777 but much roomier than a 737. It was one of the first wide-body jets flown by just two pilots, and it helped prove that twin-engine jets could safely cross oceans. Today most new 767s are built as cargo planes or military air-to-air refuelling tankers.
funFacts: In 1983 an Air Canada 767 ran out of fuel in mid-air and glided to a safe landing at an old airfield in Gimli, earning it the nickname Gimli Glider.
The 767 was the first airliner approved for 120-minute twin-engine ocean crossings, granted in 1985.
Its economy seats are usually set out 2-3-2, so almost every passenger has a window or an aisle seat.
Ansett Australia was the only airline in the world to fly 767s with a three-person cockpit that included a flight engineer.
spotterTips: Look for a wide body with two big engines and a fairly short, chunky look compared to a 777. The 767 has a slim, pointed nose and four-wheel main landing gear on each side.

melbourne.where: No longer flies passenger flights from Melbourne, but it was once a big part of Melbourne flying. Ansett Australia, which was headquartered in Melbourne, flew 767s from the 1980s until it collapsed in 2001. Qantas flew 767s from 1985 to 2014, and the very last Qantas 767 passenger flight, QF767, took off from Melbourne for Sydney on 27 December 2014.
melbourne.operators: Formerly Ansett Australia and Qantas

name: Boeing 757
engines: 2 × Pratt & Whitney PW2040 turbofans (Rolls-Royce RB211 engines were also offered)
passengers: 200 in two classes, up to 228 in one class
summary: The 757 is a long, thin, single-aisle Boeing jet with very powerful engines for its size. It can take off from short runways and hot, high airports, and it climbs very steeply. It was designed at the same time as the 767, so pilots can learn to fly both with one extra course.
funFacts: Pilots nicknamed it the Atari Ferrari because of its modern computer cockpit and its speed.
A military version called the C-32A carries the Vice President of the United States as Air Force Two.
Even though it is a single-aisle jet, air traffic controllers give the 757 extra spacing like a heavy jet because of the strong air swirls it leaves behind.
Boeing finished building the 757 in 2004 after 1,050 were made, and no direct replacement was ever built.
spotterTips: Look for a very long, narrow body standing high on tall landing gear, with a nose-up stance on the ground. Its engines look large for the size of the plane, and it has a regular low tail, not a T-tail.

photo.file: Delta 757-200 N713TW on final approach to Boston Dec 2024 2.jpg

name: Boeing 717
passengers: 106 in two classes, 117 in one class
summary: The 717 is a small jet with two engines mounted on the back of the body and a T-tail. It was the last member of the long Douglas DC-9 family, and it was perfect for short, busy routes. QantasLink flew them around Australia for 20 years before retiring them in 2024.
funFacts: It was first called the McDonnell Douglas MD-95, and was renamed the Boeing 717 after Boeing took over McDonnell Douglas in 1997.
It was the last airliner built at the old Douglas factory in Long Beach, California, where planes had been made for decades.
The final QantasLink 717 flights in late 2024 marked the end of 717 flying anywhere outside the United States.
One QantasLink 717 called The Tassie Devil had a special picture of Tasmanian devils on its side.
spotterTips: Look for two engines on the back of the body near the tail, a T-shaped tail on top of the fin, and a slim body with no engines under the wings.

melbourne.where: No longer seen in Australia. Jetstar also flew 717s from Melbourne when it started in 2004. The last QantasLink 717 flights were in October and December 2024.
melbourne.operators: Formerly QantasLink, Jetstar and Impulse Airlines

name: Embraer E195-E2
numberBuilt: 224 E-Jet E2 aircraft of all models (by late 2026)
summary: The E195-E2 is the biggest member of Embraer's newer E2 family of jets from Brazil. It has new engines, new wings and computer flight controls, so it uses much less fuel than the older E-Jets. It fills the gap between small regional jets and bigger airliners like the A320.
funFacts: Its engines are geared turbofans, which have a gearbox so the big fan at the front can spin slower than the parts behind it, making them quieter and more efficient.
The E195-E2 first flew on 29 March 2017, months earlier than Embraer had planned.
Like other E-Jets, it usually has seats in pairs either side of the aisle, so there are no middle seats.
Virgin Australia Regional Airlines flies the shorter E190-E2 sister model in Australia.
spotterTips: Look for a slim body with a double-bubble shape, big round engines under long, thin wings, and wingtips that sweep up and back without separate winglets. It is longer than the E190 and has a long, rounded nose.

melbourne.where: The E195-E2 does not fly in Australia, but its smaller sister, the E190-E2, joined Virgin Australia Regional Airlines in late 2025. It is based in Perth and flies mostly around Western Australia, with some flights to places like Adelaide and Darwin, so it is rarely seen in Victoria.
melbourne.operators: Virgin Australia Regional Airlines (E190-E2 model)

name: Bombardier CRJ900
numberBuilt: About 924 CRJ700 series aircraft of all models (CRJ700, CRJ900 and CRJ1000)
summary: The CRJ900 is a long, slim regional jet from Canada with two engines on the back of the body. It is a stretched version of the CRJ700 and is very common in North America, where it links smaller cities to big airline hubs.
funFacts: The CRJ family grew out of the Challenger business jet, so it began life as a private jet for executives.
The CRJ900 first flew on 21 February 2001, five months ahead of schedule.
Mitsubishi bought the whole CRJ programme in 2020, and the very last CRJ, a CRJ900, was delivered to SkyWest Airlines in February 2021.
There is also a business jet version called the Challenger 870.
spotterTips: Look for two engines mounted on the back of a very long, narrow body, a T-tail and small winglets. It sits low to the ground and its body looks stretched compared with its short wings.

name: BAe 146
manufacturer: British Aerospace (later Avro International and BAE Systems)
numberBuilt: 394 (221 BAe 146 plus 173 Avro RJ and RJX)
summary: The BAe 146 is a small British jet with four engines under a high wing and a T-tail. It is very quiet and can use short runways, so it was popular for city airports and for long, quiet routes across Australia. Ansett, East-West and Airlink flew many of them in Australia from the late 1980s.
funFacts: It was marketed as the Whisperjet because it is so quiet.
Instead of normal speed brakes on the wings, its tail cone splits open into two big petals to slow it down.
Having four engines on such a small airliner was unusual, and some experts thought it was a strange choice.
For several years it was the only normal jet airliner allowed to use London City Airport, which has a steep approach and a short runway.
spotterTips: Four small engines hanging under a high wing that sits on top of the body is the giveaway. Add the tall T-tail and the stubby, rounded body and it is hard to mix up with anything else.

melbourne.where: Ansett Australia, which was based in Melbourne, had 18 BAe 146s in 1999, and they were a common sight at Melbourne Airport. National Jet Express flew BAe 146 freighters for Qantas Freight until 2 October 2026, so they are now very rare in Australia.
melbourne.operators: Formerly Ansett Australia, East-West Airlines, Airlink and QantasLink, and National Jet Express

name: Fairchild Metroliner
summary: The Metroliner, usually just called the Metro, is a small, fast turboprop airliner that carries up to 19 passengers. It was built in San Antonio, Texas, and became especially popular in Australia for short regional flights and overnight freight runs.
funFacts: Almost 20 percent of all Metros ever built have flown in Australia.
It grew out of the Swearingen Merlin, a small business aeroplane.
Its tailplane can be adjusted in flight like on a big jet, which is unusual for such a small aeroplane.
Sharp Airlines still carries passengers in Metros from Essendon Fields in Melbourne.
spotterTips: Look for a very long, skinny, tube-like body with small windows and a pointed nose. It has two turboprop engines on a low wing and a cross-shaped tail where the tailplane sits partway up the fin.

melbourne.where: Sharp Airlines flies Metroliners from Essendon Fields Airport to King Island, Flinders Island and northern Tasmania, so you can see them taking off and landing at Essendon. Sharp also uses Metros on other routes around southern Australia.
melbourne.operators: Sharp Airlines

photo.file: Sharp Airlines (VH-SWK) Fairchild Swearingen SA-227DC Metro 23 at Wagga Wagga Airport.jpg

name: Beechcraft 1900
summary: The Beechcraft 1900 is a small turboprop airliner that carries 19 passengers on short regional flights. It was developed from the popular King Air business aeroplane. The later 1900D has a taller cabin so most passengers can walk upright inside.
funFacts: The 1900D is one of only two 19-seat airliners with a stand-up cabin.
It was designed to compete with the Swearingen Metro and the British Aerospace Jetstream.
The 1900D is the most popular version, with 439 built.
It has extra little fins on the tail to keep it steady, which make it look like it has wings on its tail.
spotterTips: Look for a T-tail with small extra fins, little horizontal winglets near the back of the body, and two turboprop engines on a low wing. The 1900D has a raised roof line and winglets on the main wings.

photo.file: Beech 1900D, Air New Zealand Link (Eagle Airways) JP6920497.jpg

name: McDonnell Douglas MD-11
role: Long-range three-engine wide-body freighter (formerly also an airliner)
status: In cargo service (passenger flights ended in 2014)
engines: 3 × General Electric CF6-80C2 or Pratt & Whitney PW4460 turbofans
passengers: None as a freighter (the passenger version carried about 298 in three classes)
summary: The MD-11 is a big three-engine jet, with one engine on each wing and a third built into the tail. It started as a passenger airliner developed from the DC-10, but today it flies only as a cargo plane. All MD-11s were grounded in late 2025 after an accident, then cleared to fly again in May 2026.
funFacts: It was the last new airliner design from McDonnell Douglas before the company joined Boeing in 1997.
The last MD-11 passenger flight was flown by the Dutch airline KLM on 26 October 2014.
It has small winglets that point both up and down at the wingtips.
FedEx planned to keep flying its MD-11 freighters until about 2032.
spotterTips: Look for the third engine built into the base of the tail fin, above the back of the body. It looks like a DC-10 but is longer and has small winglets on the wingtips.

name: Airbus A300
role: Wide-body airliner, now mostly a freighter
status: In cargo service (very few passenger aircraft left)
engines: 2 × General Electric CF6-80C2 or Pratt & Whitney PW4158 turbofans
passengers: None as a freighter (the A300-600R passenger version carried about 247 in two classes)
summary: The A300 was the very first Airbus and the first wide-body airliner with only two engines. It started the Airbus company on the path to becoming one of the world's two biggest aeroplane makers. Today most surviving A300s fly as cargo planes.
funFacts: It was the world's first twin-engine wide-body airliner.
Trans Australia Airlines, which was headquartered in Melbourne, flew A300s from the early 1980s and was the first Australian domestic airline to buy a wide-body jet.
The Airbus Beluga transport plane was built using the A300-600 as its starting point.
Airbus delivered the last A300 in July 2007.
spotterTips: Look for a wide body with two big engines, a rounded nose and a fairly short, stubby look compared with newer Airbus wide-bodies. Freighters have few or no windows and a big cargo door on the left side behind the wing or near the front.

melbourne.where: No longer flies regularly in Victoria. Trans Australia Airlines (later Australian Airlines), which was headquartered in Melbourne, flew A300s on domestic routes from the early 1980s, including Perth to Melbourne. They were replaced by Boeing 767s after Qantas took over the airline.
melbourne.operators: Formerly Trans Australia Airlines and Australian Airlines

name: Ilyushin Il-76
status: In service and still in production
summary: The Il-76 is a big four-engine cargo plane designed in the Soviet Union to carry heavy loads into rough airfields. It has a high wing, a T-tail and a ramp at the back for loading vehicles. Many countries use it as a military transport and for cargo charters.
funFacts: It was designed to land on unpaved runways, which made it useful in places without proper airports.
Special versions have been used to train cosmonauts in weightlessness by flying up-and-down curves.
The Il-78 air-to-air refuelling tanker and the A-50 radar plane are both based on the Il-76.
Most Il-76s were built in Tashkent in Uzbekistan, and the newest version is built in Ulyanovsk, Russia.
spotterTips: Look for four engines under a high wing, a T-tail, and lots of wheels on the main landing gear. Older versions have a glass-windowed nose under the cockpit for a navigator.

name: Airbus Beluga (A300-600ST)
role: Outsize cargo transport for aircraft parts
status: In service but being retired (the first was retired in January 2026)
summary: The Beluga is a huge, whale-shaped cargo plane built from an Airbus A300 with a giant bubble on top. Airbus used it to fly big aeroplane parts, like wings and body sections, between its factories in Europe. It is now being replaced by the even bigger Beluga XL.
funFacts: Its main cargo hold is bigger than that of the giant Antonov An-124 and the Lockheed C-5 Galaxy.
The cockpit sits lower than the cargo hold, so the whole nose can swing up to load cargo straight in.
It replaced Airbus's older Super Guppy transport planes, the last of which retired in 1997.
Only five were ever built.
spotterTips: You cannot miss it. Look for a huge bulging upper body like a whale, with the cockpit tucked low under the front, and extra fins on the ends of the tailplane.

photo.file: Hamburg-Finkenwerder Airport Airbus Transport International Airbus A300B4-608ST F-GSTD (DSC09656).jpg

name: Northrop Grumman MQ-4C Triton
numberBuilt: Not published (the RAAF has received 3 of 4 ordered)
crew: None on board. 4 people fly it from a ground station
summary: The Triton is a large drone with no pilot on board that flies very high over the ocean for more than a day at a time. It uses radar and cameras to watch huge areas of sea. The US Navy and the Royal Australian Air Force both fly it.
funFacts: It can stay in the air for about 30 hours on a single flight.
Its wingspan of almost 40 metres is wider than a Boeing 737's, even though its body is only about 14.5 metres long.
Australia was the first country outside the United States to order it, announced in 2014.
It works as a team with the RAAF's P-8A Poseidon, with the Triton watching wide areas and the crewed P-8A doing closer work.
spotterTips: It is hard to see from the ground because it flies so high. Look for very long, thin wings, a bulging nose with no cockpit windows, a single engine on top of the back of the body, and a V-shaped tail.

melbourne.where: Not based in Victoria. The RAAF's Tritons are flown by No. 9 Squadron from RAAF Base Edinburgh in South Australia and RAAF Base Tindal in the Northern Territory. The first RAAF Triton arrived in Australia on 16 June 2024.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force

photo.file: MQ-4C Triton Test Flight with Multi-Intelligence Upgrade.jpg

name: Leonardo C-27J Spartan
status: In service (the RAAF announced in 2026 that it will retire its fleet)
crew: 2 pilots, plus a loadmaster when needed
summary: The C-27J Spartan is a twin-engine military transport from Italy that can carry troops, vehicles and supplies into short, rough airstrips. It is smaller than a C-130 Hercules but shares the same type of engines. The RAAF received 10 Spartans between 2015 and 2018.
funFacts: It uses the same Rolls-Royce AE2100 engines and six-bladed propellers as the C-130J Hercules.
It is agile enough to perform loops and barrel rolls at air shows, which is rare for a transport aircraft.
The US Air Force retired its brand new C-27Js after only a short time in 2012 and 2013, and they were passed on to the US Coast Guard and special forces.
In April 2026 Australia announced it would retire its 10 Spartans early and replace them with other aircraft.
spotterTips: Look for a high wing with two turboprop engines, each with six curved propeller blades, and a tall tail above an upswept rear body with a loading ramp. It looks like a shrunken Hercules with only two engines.

melbourne.where: Not based in Victoria, but RAAF Spartans have often appeared at the Australian International Airshow at Avalon near Geelong, including a flying display in March 2025. The RAAF plans to retire them, so they will become harder to see.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (No. 35 Squadron)

name: McDonnell Douglas F/A-18 Hornet
status: In service with some countries (retired by the RAAF in 2021)
crew: 1 pilot (2 in the two-seat B and D models)
summary: The F/A-18 Hornet is a twin-engine fighter first built for the US Navy to fly from aircraft carriers. The F/A in its name means it can be both a fighter and an attack aircraft. The RAAF flew 75 of them from 1985 to 2021, before replacing them with the F-35A.
funFacts: Most of the RAAF's Hornets were assembled at the Government Aircraft Factories plant at Avalon Airport in Victoria, and their engines were built at Fishermans Bend in Melbourne.
Australia's Hornets had the catapult hook on the nose wheel removed, because the RAAF does not fly from aircraft carriers.
After retiring them, Australia sold 25 Hornets to Canada, and some are still flying there.
The newer Super Hornet looks similar but is about 25 percent bigger and is mostly a new design.
spotterTips: Look for twin tall tail fins that lean outwards, two engines side by side, and long strakes running from the wings forward along the sides of the cockpit. The wings have square-cut tips that often carry missiles.

melbourne.where: RAAF classic Hornets retired in 2021, but you can see a real one, F/A-18A A21-43, in the Strike Hangar at the RAAF Museum at Point Cook. The RAAF's Hornets were also assembled at Avalon Airport near Geelong and were regular performers at the Australian International Airshow at Avalon.
melbourne.operators: Formerly the Royal Australian Air Force (now on display at the RAAF Museum, Point Cook)

photo.file: A21-22 McDonnell Douglas F-A-18A Hornet RAAF (7017328933).jpg

name: McDonnell Douglas F-15 Eagle
status: In service (the US Air Force is retiring its older F-15C and F-15D models)
numberBuilt: 1,198 F-15A/B/C/D/J/DJ (not counting the later F-15E family)
summary: The F-15 Eagle is a large, powerful American fighter built to win control of the sky. It can fly at more than twice the speed of sound and was the main US Air Force fighter for many years. Newer versions such as the F-15E and F-15EX are still being used and built.
funFacts: It is one of the most successful fighters ever, with more than 100 air combat victories and no losses in air-to-air combat.
In 1983 an Israeli F-15 lost most of one wing in a mid-air collision and the pilot still landed it safely.
An F-15 was once used to launch a missile that reached space to test hitting a satellite.
Australia looked at the F-15 when choosing a new fighter in the late 1970s, but picked the F/A-18 Hornet instead.
spotterTips: Look for a big fighter with two upright tail fins, two engines side by side, large square air intakes beside the cockpit and a wide, flat wing. Its bubble canopy sits high on the nose.

photo.file: F-15C Eagle from the 44th Fighter Squadron flies during a routine training exercise April 15, 2019.jpg

name: McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom II
summary: The F-4 Phantom II is a big, powerful two-seat jet fighter from the Cold War era that could fly at more than twice the speed of sound. It served with the US Air Force, Navy and Marines and with 11 other countries, and a few air forces such as Greece and Turkey still fly it more than 65 years after its first flight.
funFacts: It is the only aircraft that has been flown by both famous American display teams, the US Air Force Thunderbirds and the US Navy Blue Angels.
Production ended with 5,195 built, including 138 made in Japan by Mitsubishi.
The RAAF leased 24 brand-new F-4Es from 1970 to 1973 while it waited for its delayed F-111 bombers.
Old Phantoms were turned into remote-controlled target drones, and the US Air Force kept flying them that way until December 2016.
spotterTips: Look for a bulky two-seat jet with wingtips that bend upwards, a tailplane that slopes sharply downwards, two smoky engines side by side and big air intakes beside the cockpit.

melbourne.where: An F-4E is on display at the RAAF Museum at Point Cook, painted to look like one of the 24 Phantoms the RAAF leased from the US Air Force between 1970 and 1973. The aircraft itself was a US Air Force jet presented to the museum in 1990.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force No. 1 and No. 6 Squadrons (No. 82 Wing) at RAAF Base Amberley, Queensland, from 1970 to 1973.

name: Mikoyan MiG-29
manufacturer: Mikoyan (now part of United Aircraft Corporation)
summary: The MiG-29 is a nimble twin-engine fighter designed in the Soviet Union during the 1970s. It was built to win close air battles and was sold to air forces all over the world, including India, Algeria and Ukraine. More than 1,600 have been made.
funFacts: When taxiing and taking off it can close its main air intakes and breathe through louvres on top of the body, so it does not suck up stones from rough runways.
Fulcrum is the code name NATO gave it, but some Soviet pilots liked the name so much that they started using it themselves.
It is built to handle 9 g, which means the pilot briefly feels nine times heavier than normal in tight turns.
After Germany reunited, German pilots flew ex-East German MiG-29s and found them more agile at slow speeds than several Western fighters.
spotterTips: Look for two widely spaced engines with square air intakes under the wings, two tail fins that lean slightly outwards, and long curved wing extensions running forward beside the cockpit.

name: Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk
status: Retired from combat in 2008, but a few still fly for training
summary: The F-117 Nighthawk was the world's first operational aircraft designed from the start to be stealthy, meaning very hard to see on radar. Its odd shape is made of flat angled panels that bounce radar waves away. It left combat service in 2008, but a few still fly to help train other pilots.
funFacts: It was so secret that the US Air Force did not admit it existed until 10 November 1988, five years after it entered service.
Its designers used a computer program called Echo to work out how flat panels, called facets, could scatter radar signals away from the receiver.
Even though its name starts with F for fighter, it was really an attack aircraft that carried bombs inside its body and had no guns.
It was nicknamed the Wobblin' Goblin, although pilots who flew it say it handled perfectly well.
spotterTips: Unmistakable: a jet-black aeroplane made of flat triangular panels, like a folded paper aeroplane, with a V-shaped tail and very sharply swept wings.

name: Rockwell B-1 Lancer
crew: 4 (aircraft commander, pilot, offensive systems officer and defensive systems officer)
summary: The B-1 Lancer is a big American bomber with swing wings that move forward for take-off and sweep back for high-speed flight. It can fly faster than sound and carries a very heavy load inside its body. The US Air Force has flown it since 1986.
funFacts: Its nickname Bone came from a newspaper story that spelled B-1 as B-ONE, and the name stuck.
The first version, the B-1A, was cancelled after just four were built. The design was revived in the 1980s as the B-1B, and 100 were made.
It has three bomb bays inside its body that can hold about 34,000 kg of weapons.
It was first built to carry nuclear weapons, but it was later changed to carry only ordinary (conventional) weapons.
spotterTips: Look for a long, sleek bomber with a pointed nose, a smoothly blended body, wings that can sweep back, and four engines in two pairs under the body.

name: Boeing KC-46 Pegasus
crew: 3 (2 pilots and 1 boom operator), with 15 extra seats for other crew
passengers: Up to 54 (up to 114 in an emergency), or 58 patients
summary: The KC-46 Pegasus is a flying fuel station based on the Boeing 767 airliner. It passes fuel to other military aircraft in mid-air so they can fly much further without landing. It can also carry cargo, passengers or patients.
funFacts: It mixes parts from several different 767 models, including the body of one, the wings of another and the flight deck of a third.
It can refuel aircraft in two ways: with a long stiff boom steered into the other aircraft, or with a hose and basket for aircraft fitted with a probe.
It can give away about 94,000 kg of fuel to other aircraft.
As well as the US Air Force, it is flown by Japan and Israel.
spotterTips: It looks like a grey Boeing 767 airliner with only a few windows, a refuelling boom folded up under the tail, and small hose pods under the wings.

photo.file: KC-46 Pegasus prepares to refuel C-17 (cropped).jpg

name: Boeing E-3 Sentry
specsVariant: E-3 with TF33 engines (first flight date is for the EC-137D test aircraft)
crew: 4 flight crew plus 13 to 19 mission crew
summary: The E-3 Sentry is a flying radar station built from a Boeing 707 airliner. The huge spinning disc on its back holds a radar that can watch the sky for hundreds of kilometres, and the crew inside direct other aircraft. It has been used by the US Air Force, NATO, France, Saudi Arabia and Chile.
funFacts: The disc on its back, called a rotodome, is about 9.1 metres wide and 1.8 metres thick, and it turns six times every minute.
The rotodome sits on two struts about 3.4 metres above the body of the aeroplane.
It can stay in the air for more than 8 hours without refuelling, and much longer if it is refuelled in flight.
Only 68 were built, and production ended in 1992. The British Royal Air Force retired its E-3s in 2021.
spotterTips: Look for an old-style four-engine Boeing 707 shape with a giant round disc mounted on two legs above the rear of the body.

photo.file: E-3 Sentry Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) conducts a mission.jpg

name: Panavia Tornado
manufacturer: Panavia Aircraft (BAE Systems, Airbus and Leonardo)
specsVariant: Tornado IDS (wingspan with wings at 25 degrees)
summary: The Tornado is a two-seat swing-wing jet built by Britain, Germany and Italy working together. It was designed to fly very fast and very low to attack targets on the ground, and a fighter version was made too. It is still flying in 2026, more than 50 years after the first prototype took off.
funFacts: Its wings swing forward for slow flying and landing, and sweep back for high-speed flight.
Unusually for a fighter jet, its engines have thrust reversers, like an airliner, which help it stop on short runways.
It came in three main versions: 745 IDS strike jets, 194 ADV air defence fighters and 51 ECR jets for attacking enemy radars.
The British Royal Air Force retired its Tornados in 2019, but Germany and Saudi Arabia have kept theirs flying.
spotterTips: Look for a slim two-seat jet with a single tall tail fin, two engines side by side, and wings that may be spread out or swept back depending on its speed.

name: Chengdu J-20
engines: 2 × Shenyang WS-10C afterburning turbofans (newer aircraft use the WS-15)
summary: The J-20 is China's stealth fighter, designed to be hard to spot on radar. It first flew in 2011 and joined the People's Liberation Army Air Force in 2017. Much about it is still secret, so many of its figures are estimates.
funFacts: Its Chinese name Weilong means Mighty Dragon.
At about 21 metres long it is bigger than most fighters, longer even than the American F-22 Raptor.
It has small extra wings near the front, called canards, an idea Chengdu had used on earlier designs.
About 500 had been built by the middle of 2026.
spotterTips: Look for a long, dark grey jet with small canard wings behind the cockpit, a delta-shaped main wing, two angled tail fins and a large bubble canopy.

name: General Dynamics F-111
role: Swing-wing strike bomber and reconnaissance aircraft
numberBuilt: 563 of all versions (including 24 F-111Cs built for Australia)
specsVariant: F-111C (RAAF version, wingspan with wings spread)
crew: 2 (pilot and weapon systems officer, side by side)
summary: The F-111 was a fast swing-wing bomber that could race along close to the ground at night or in bad weather. Australia flew F-111s for 37 years and they became one of the most famous aircraft in RAAF history. The RAAF was the last air force in the world to fly them, retiring them in 2010.
funFacts: The RAAF accepted its first F-111Cs in 1968, but technical problems kept them grounded, so they did not arrive in Australia until 1973.
Australians nicknamed it the Pig because of its long snout and the way it could follow the ground at low level with its special radar.
Instead of ejection seats, the two crew sat side by side in a capsule. In an emergency the whole cockpit flew away and came down by parachute.
It could fly at about 2.5 times the speed of sound at high altitude.
spotterTips: Look for a long, pointed nose, two crew seated side by side under a wide canopy, swing wings, and two engines at the back with a single tall tail fin.

melbourne.where: The RAAF Museum at Point Cook displays F-111G A8-272, and the Australian National Aviation Museum at Moorabbin Airport has the cockpit module from F-111C A8-131.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force No. 1 and No. 6 Squadrons at RAAF Base Amberley, Queensland, from 1973 until 3 December 2010.

photo.file: AFR F-111 air to air refueling.jpg

name: Dassault Mirage III
manufacturer: Dassault Aviation (licence-built in Australia by the Government Aircraft Factories)
specsVariant: Mirage IIIE (the Australian Mirage IIIO was very similar)
crew: 1 pilot (2 in the Mirage IIID trainer)
summary: The Mirage III is a French jet fighter with a large triangle-shaped delta wing and no tailplane. It could fly at more than twice the speed of sound, and Australia built its own Mirages in Melbourne. They were the RAAF's main fighter from the 1960s until 1988.
funFacts: Australia's Mirages were assembled at Fishermans Bend in Melbourne, with the Commonwealth Aircraft Corporation building their Atar engines under licence.
The Australian factory built three versions: 48 interceptors, 50 ground attack jets and 16 two-seat trainers.
After the RAAF retired its Mirages in 1988, Pakistan bought 50 of them, and Pakistan is the last country still flying the Mirage III.
It has no horizontal tail at all. The back edge of the big delta wing does the job instead.
spotterTips: Look for a slim jet with a big triangular delta wing, no tailplane, a single tall tail fin and half-moon shaped air intakes beside the cockpit.

melbourne.where: Australian Mirages were built by the Government Aircraft Factories at Fishermans Bend. The RAAF Museum at Point Cook displays Mirage A3-92, and the Australian National Aviation Museum at Moorabbin Airport has Mirage A3-45.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force fighter squadrons from the 1960s until 1988.

photo.file: Two Mirage III of the Royal Australian Air Force 1.JPEG

name: CAC Sabre
engines: 1 × Rolls-Royce Avon 26 turbojet (built under licence by CAC)
summary: The CAC Sabre was an Australian version of the American F-86 Sabre jet fighter, built in Melbourne. CAC gave it a more powerful British Rolls-Royce Avon engine, which gave it much more power than the American original. It served with the RAAF from 1954 to 1971.
funFacts: Fitting the bigger Avon engine meant CAC had to redesign much of the body, so it was quite different from the American Sabre.
Only 112 were built: one prototype and 111 production aircraft.
No. 76 Squadron flew Sabres in an aerobatic team called the Black Panthers.
After the RAAF retired them, Sabres went on to serve with Malaysia, and 23 were given to Indonesia between 1973 and 1975.
spotterTips: Look for a silver single-engine jet with a round air intake right in the nose, swept-back wings, a bubble canopy and a swept tail.

melbourne.where: Designed and built by CAC at Fishermans Bend. The RAAF Museum at Point Cook displays the prototype CA-26 Sabre A94-101, and the Australian National Aviation Museum at Moorabbin Airport has CA-27 Sabre A94-910.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force No. 3, 75, 76, 77 and 79 Squadrons from 1954 to 1971, including service in Malaysia and Thailand.

photo.file: Royal Australian Air Force, on loan to the Temora Aviation Museum, (VH-IPN, former military registration A94-983) CAC Sabre Mk.32 landing at Avalon during the 2015 Australian International Airshow.jpg

name: CAC Winjeel
role: Pilot trainer and forward air control aircraft
engines: 1 × Pratt & Whitney R-985 Wasp Junior 445 hp nine-cylinder radial piston engine
crew: 2 (instructor and student), with space for a third seat
summary: The Winjeel is a sturdy propeller trainer designed and built in Melbourne by the Commonwealth Aircraft Corporation. RAAF pilots learned to fly in it from 1955, and later it was used to mark targets with smoke for other aircraft. It served for 40 years before retiring in 1995.
funFacts: Its name comes from a Victorian Aboriginal word meaning young eagle, another spelling of Bunjil.
It was designed to replace two famous trainers at once, the Tiger Moth and the Wirraway.
In its later career it carried smoke bombs to mark targets on the ground for attack aircraft, a job called forward air control.
The RAAF heritage squadron at Point Cook still flies Winjeel A85-439.
spotterTips: Look for a chunky single-engine propeller aeroplane with a big round radial engine at the front, a large glasshouse canopy, fixed landing gear and a tall, square-ish tail.

melbourne.where: Designed and built by CAC at Fishermans Bend. The RAAF Museum at Point Cook displays Winjeel A85-401, and No. 100 Squadron flies A85-439 from Point Cook. The Australian National Aviation Museum at Moorabbin has A85-418, and A85-405 is the gate guard at RAAF Base East Sale.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force pilot training schools from 1955, and forward air control units until 1994. Today No. 100 Squadron (Air Force Heritage Squadron) and private owners keep some flying.

name: de Havilland Canada DHC-4 Caribou
engines: 2 × Pratt & Whitney R-2000 Twin Wasp 1,450 hp 14-cylinder radial piston engines
summary: The Caribou is a tough twin-engine transport that can take off and land on very short, rough airstrips. It carried troops and supplies in places where bigger aeroplanes could not go, including during the Vietnam War. The RAAF flew Caribous for about 45 years until 2009.
funFacts: It could operate from a runway only about 365 metres long.
The US Army bought 159 and was the largest user. A Caribou could carry two Jeeps through its rear loading ramp.

In 1975, during a civil war in Portuguese Timor, 44 people took over an RAAF Caribou on a Red Cross mission and asked to be flown to Darwin. The crew flew them there and they were later given refugee visas.
That same Caribou, A4-140, became the RAAF's very last one. It retired on 27 November 2009 and was given to the Australian War Memorial.
spotterTips: Look for a high wing with a bend (gull shape) near the body, two big round radial engines, a tall tail and a back end that sweeps up to a large rear loading ramp.

melbourne.where: The RAAF Museum at Point Cook displays Caribou A4-152, which was given to the museum in November 2009. The RAAF's last Caribou, A4-140, is at the Australian War Memorial in Canberra.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force (including No. 38 Squadron) from the 1960s until 2009, with service in the Vietnam War.

name: Pilatus PC-9
manufacturer: Pilatus Aircraft (RAAF PC-9/A mostly built under licence by Hawker de Havilland in Australia)
engines: 1 × Pratt & Whitney Canada PT6A-62 turboprop (857 kW)
crew: 1 or 2 pilots (instructor and student sit one behind the other)
summary: The PC-9 is a fast Swiss turboprop trainer used to teach military pilots before they move on to jets. The RAAF flew it for about 30 years, and the Roulettes aerobatic team flew it in shows all over Australia. The RAAF replaced it with the PC-21 in 2019, but other air forces still use it.
funFacts: The RAAF ordered 67 PC-9/As in 1985, and 48 of them were built under licence in Australia by Hawker de Havilland.
The Roulettes flew PC-9s painted bright red, white and blue, and the RAAF later painted almost all its PC-9s in those colours so any aircraft could join the team.
The American T-6 Texan II trainer was developed from the PC-9.
The last RAAF pilot course to fly PC-9s graduated on 6 December 2019.
spotterTips: Look for a sleek single-engine propeller aeroplane with a long pointed nose, a bubble canopy with two seats one behind the other, and retractable landing gear. RAAF ones were red, white and blue.

melbourne.where: RAAF Base East Sale in Gippsland, home of the Roulettes, has two PC-9s (A23-030 and A23-036) as gate guardians. The RAAF Museum at Point Cook holds A23-001, the first RAAF PC-9/A. The Roulettes flew PC-9s at shows around Victoria until 2019.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force pilot training units, including the Roulettes at RAAF Base East Sale, from the late 1980s until 2019.

photo.file: RAAF Pilatus PC-9A Roulettes CBR Gilbert.jpg

name: de Havilland Mosquito
manufacturer: de Havilland (also built in Canada and Australia)
role: Fast bomber, fighter-bomber, night fighter and photo-reconnaissance aircraft
engines: 2 × Rolls-Royce Merlin 76/77 1,710 hp V-12 piston engines
summary: The Mosquito was a fast British twin-engine aircraft of the Second World War, made mostly from wood. It was so quick that it first went to war as a bomber with no guns at all, relying on speed to escape. It was used for bombing, night fighting and taking photographs from high above.
funFacts: Its body and wings were made mainly of wood, such as birch plywood and spruce, which is why it was called the Wooden Wonder.
De Havilland Australia built 212 Mosquitos in Sydney, and the RAAF flew them in the Pacific.
After the war, RAAF photo-reconnaissance Mosquitos kept mapping Australia from the air until 1953.
About 30 survive on display around the world, and five can still fly.
spotterTips: Look for a slim, smooth twin-engine aeroplane with two Merlin engines close to a short, rounded body, a small glazed nose and a cockpit set well forward.

melbourne.where: De Havilland Australia built 212 Mosquitos in Sydney. The RAAF Museum at Point Cook holds photo-reconnaissance Mosquito A52-600 in its collection, although it is kept in storage rather than on public display.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force squadrons in the Pacific during the Second World War, and photo-survey flights over Australia until 1953.

name: Avro Anson
role: Maritime patrol aircraft and aircrew trainer
engines: 2 × Armstrong Siddeley Cheetah IX 335 hp seven-cylinder radial piston engines
summary: The Avro Anson was a reliable British twin-engine aeroplane first used to patrol the coast and later to train thousands of aircrew in the Second World War. Air forces in Britain, Canada and Australia flew huge numbers of them. After the war many became small airliners and charter planes.
funFacts: It was named after the British admiral George Anson.
More than 11,000 were built, and production carried on until 1952.
The RAAF operated 1,028 Ansons, which stayed in service until 1955.
In 1940 two RAAF Ansons collided in mid-air over New South Wales and became stuck together, one on top of the other. The pilot of the top aircraft managed to land them safely near Brocklesby.
spotterTips: Look for a low-wing twin-engine aeroplane with two round radial engines, a row of square cabin windows along the side, and a gun turret on top of the body on wartime versions.

melbourne.where: In Victoria you can see Anson W2364 at the Nhill Aviation Heritage Centre, and the Avro Anson Museum in Ballarat is restoring Anson LV284.
melbourne.operators: Royal Australian Air Force, from 1936 until 1955, for coastal patrol and training aircrew.

name: Mitsubishi A6M Zero
engines: 1 × Nakajima Sakae 12 940 hp 14-cylinder radial piston engine
summary: The Zero was Japan's main navy fighter in the Second World War, flown from aircraft carriers and land bases. It was very light, could turn tightly and could fly extremely long distances. Early in the Pacific war it surprised Allied pilots, but newer Allied fighters later overtook it.
funFacts: Its name comes from Type 0, because it entered service in the Japanese Imperial year 2600, which was 1940.
The Allied code name Zeke was given to it by an intelligence unit based at Eagle Farm in Brisbane.
With an extra fuel tank it could fly about 3,100 km, an amazing distance for a single-seat fighter of its time.
Most Zeros that fly today have American engines, and only one, at the Planes of Fame Air Museum in California, still has an original Sakae engine.
spotterTips: Look for a slim single-seat fighter with a round radial engine at the front, long rounded wingtips, a long glasshouse canopy and a slender tail.

melbourne.where: Thirty-six Zeros escorted the Japanese air raid on Darwin on 19 February 1942. The Australian War Memorial in Canberra displays a restored A6M2 Zero, and the Australian Aviation Heritage Centre in Darwin shows the wreckage of another.
melbourne.operators: Imperial Japanese Navy Air Service only.

name: Tupolev Tu-144
status: Retired (passenger service ended in 1978 and the last flight was in 1999)
summary: The Tu-144 was the Soviet Union's supersonic airliner and the first passenger jet ever to fly faster than sound. It looked so much like the Anglo-French Concorde that people nicknamed it Concordski. It only carried paying passengers for a few months before being withdrawn.
funFacts: It first flew on 31 December 1968, about two months before Concorde, making it the first supersonic airliner to take to the air.
The cabin was so noisy at cruise that passengers sitting two seats apart sometimes had to pass handwritten notes to talk to each other.
Its top speed was more than twice the speed of sound, around 2,500 km/h.
In the late 1990s NASA and Tupolev turned one Tu-144 into a flying laboratory to research future supersonic airliners.
spotterTips: Look for a long, pointed body with a big delta (triangle) wing set low, a nose that droops down for landing, and four engines grouped in two large boxes under the wing. Later versions have small extra wings called canards that fold out just behind the cockpit.

name: McDonnell Douglas DC-10
status: Retired from passenger service, with a few still flying as cargo aircraft and firefighting air tankers
summary: The DC-10 is a big wide-body airliner with three engines, one under each wing and one in the tail. It carried passengers around the world from the 1970s, and today a few still work as cargo planes and giant firefighting air tankers.
funFacts: The US Air Force turned the DC-10 into the KC-10 Extender, a flying fuel tanker that refuelled other aircraft in mid-air. Sixty were built.
A DC-10 air tanker can drop around 45,000 litres of water or fire retardant in one load.
The charity Orbis flew a DC-10 as a Flying Eye Hospital, with an operating theatre inside where doctors treated patients and trained local eye surgeons.
The tail engine sits in a straight tube that goes right through the bottom of the tail fin.
spotterTips: Count the engines: one under each wing and a third mounted high in the tail, with the tail fin sitting on top of the engine pod. The tail engine looks like a straight tube running through the fin, unlike the TriStar, whose tail engine is fed by an intake at the base of the fin.

melbourne.where: DC-10 air tankers have fought Australian bushfires. One was based at Avalon Airport near Geelong for the 2009 to 2010 fire season, and in the 2015 to 2016 season a DC-10 nicknamed Southern Belle was based at RAAF Base Richmond in New South Wales before moving to Avalon.
melbourne.operators: 10 Tanker Air Carrier, a US firefighting company, on contract during Australian bushfire seasons

name: Lockheed L-1011 TriStar
status: Retired from airline service, with one still flying as a rocket launcher
summary: The TriStar was Lockheed's three-engine wide-body airliner and the great rival of the DC-10. It was packed with clever technology for its time, but only 250 were built and it was the last airliner Lockheed ever made.
funFacts: It was the first wide-body airliner certified to land itself in zero visibility, with the autopilot doing the whole landing.
One TriStar called Stargazer still flies today. It carries Pegasus rockets under its belly and drops them high in the sky, where the rocket fires and climbs into orbit.
Problems developing its Rolls-Royce RB211 engines helped push Rolls-Royce into bankruptcy in 1971, and the British and US governments had to step in to save the project.
Its name comes from its three engines, which form a tri star pattern.
spotterTips: Look for three engines: one under each wing and one in the tail. The tail engine is buried inside the rear of the body, with an air intake at the base of the fin and an S-shaped duct, so the fin looks smooth and the engine exhaust comes out at the very back.

photo.file: 11df - Delta Air Lines Lockheed L-1011 TriStar 1; N1732D@FLL;30.01.1998 (5016025629).jpg

name: Boeing 727
status: Retired by Australian airlines, with a few still in cargo, military and private use overseas
summary: The Boeing 727 is a three-engine jet airliner built for shorter routes and smaller airports. It brought jet travel to Australian domestic flights in 1964, and for many years it was one of the most common airliners in the world.
funFacts: The first two 727s in Australia, one for Ansett and one for TAA, landed at Essendon Airport in Melbourne on 16 October 1964.
It has three engines because the airlines could not agree. One wanted four engines, another wanted two, and a third needed three for flights over water.

In 1971 a hijacker known as D.B. Cooper jumped out of a 727's rear stairs with a parachute and was never found. Boeing then added a small flap called the Cooper vane so the stairs could not be opened in flight.
The 727 is so loud that it has been banned from some Australian airports, even with noise-reducing hush kits fitted.
spotterTips: Look for three engines all at the back: one on each side of the rear body and one in the tail, fed by an intake on top of the fuselage in front of the fin. It has a T-tail, with the horizontal tail on top of the fin, and a low swept wing with no engines on it.

melbourne.where: The 727 started Australia's domestic jet age. The first two arrived at Essendon Airport on 16 October 1964 and began passenger flights on 2 November 1964. TAA (later Australian Airlines) flew them until 1992 and Ansett until 1997, so they were a common sight at Essendon and later Tullamarine.
melbourne.operators: Ansett and TAA (historic)

name: GAF Nomad
role: Twin-engine utility and short take-off transport
status: Production ended in 1985, with only a few still flying
summary: The Nomad is a small twin-engine turboprop that was designed and built in Melbourne. It could take off and land on short, rough airstrips, so it was used by the Australian Army, the RAAF, Customs and the Royal Flying Doctor Service.
funFacts: The first prototype flew from Avalon Airport in Victoria in July 1971, and production aircraft were built at Fishermans Bend in Melbourne.
The longer N24 version could carry 16 passengers, four more than the original N22.
A coastal patrol version called the Searchmaster was used to watch Australia's northern coastline.
In 2008 GippsAero in Victoria bought the rights to the design and planned to revive it, but the project was dropped by 2021.
spotterTips: The Nomad has a high wing braced by struts, two turboprop engines on the wing and a boxy body with a square-ish cross section. Its main wheels fold into bulges on the sides of the lower fuselage, and it has a single tall tail fin.

melbourne.where: The Nomad is a true Victorian aeroplane. It was built by Government Aircraft Factories at Fishermans Bend in Melbourne and first flew at Avalon. The Moorabbin Air Museum has a former RAAF Nomad (A18-316) that is being restored.
melbourne.operators: Historically the Australian Army, RAAF, Australian Customs Coastwatch and the Royal Flying Doctor Service

name: GippsAero GA8 Airvan
status: In service, with production restarted in 2025
numberBuilt: About 262 by 2020, with new aircraft being built again since 2025
summary: The Airvan is a tough, boxy eight-seat aeroplane designed and built in the Latrobe Valley in Victoria. It is used for carrying people and cargo to remote airstrips, for skydiving and for jobs like surveying. Production stopped in 2020 but restarted in 2025 after one of the original founders bought the company back.
funFacts: In 2010 an Airvan became the first Australian-designed aircraft to fly all the way around the world.
It can take off from an airstrip only about 300 metres long in normal conditions.
For a few years it was called the Mahindra Airvan 8, after the Indian company Mahindra bought GippsAero.
When production restarted in June 2025, the first new aircraft was serial number 263, the first new Airvan in five years.
spotterTips: Look for a high wing held up by struts, a single propeller, fixed landing gear and a tall, square-looking body that is almost like a flying van. It has a large sliding door on the side for loading cargo or letting skydivers jump out.

melbourne.where: Airvans are built at GippsAero's factory at Latrobe Regional Airport in Morwell, about two hours east of Melbourne, where production restarted in June 2025. You may also see them at country airfields and skydiving centres around Victoria.
melbourne.operators: GippsAero (manufacturer), skydiving clubs, charter and survey operators
