name: Pilatus PC-24
role: Light business jet and air ambulance
summary: The PC-24 is a small business jet from Switzerland that is tough enough to land on short grass and dirt runways. That makes it perfect for the Royal Flying Doctor Service, which uses it as a fast air ambulance to carry patients long distances across Australia.
funFacts: It is certified to use grass, wet earth and snow-covered runways, which is very unusual for a jet.
Pilatus says it was the first business jet fitted with a big cargo door that fits a standard pallet.
The first PC-24 air ambulance was handed over to the Royal Flying Doctor Service in Western Australia in November 2018.
It can be flown by a single pilot, even though it is a jet.
spotterTips: Look for a low wing, a T-tail and two jet engines mounted high on the back of the body. A good clue is the large square cargo door on the left side behind the wing. Flying Doctor jets are white with the red RFDS markings.

melbourne.where: Royal Flying Doctor Service PC-24 jets from Adelaide sometimes bring patients into Essendon Fields. Privately owned and charter PC-24s also visit Essendon Fields and Melbourne Airport.
melbourne.operators: Royal Flying Doctor Service (Central Operations in Adelaide and Western Operations in Western Australia), charter operators and private owners

name: Cessna 152
status: Out of production since 1985, but many still fly
summary: The Cessna 152 is a small two-seat aeroplane that a huge number of pilots have learned to fly in. It was built from 1977 to 1985, but it is so simple and reliable that flight schools still use it every day.
funFacts: It replaced the earlier Cessna 150 and was designed to run on the low-lead aviation fuel that was becoming standard.
Some 152s were built in France by Reims Aviation and are called F152s.
The student and instructor sit side by side, so the instructor can watch everything the student does.
More than 7,500 were built in only about nine years.
spotterTips: It looks like a smaller Cessna 172: a high wing with one strut on each side, a single propeller and a nose wheel. The cabin is short with only one row of two seats, and the windows end not far behind the doors.

melbourne.where: Moorabbin Airport is the best place to see them, flying circuits with student pilots. They also fly from Lilydale and other training airfields around Victoria.
melbourne.operators: Flight schools and aero clubs, plus private owners

name: Cessna 182 Skylane
summary: The Cessna 182 Skylane is a bigger, more powerful cousin of the Cessna 172. It can carry four people and their bags further and faster, and it is popular for touring, skydiving and aerial work.
funFacts: Its high wing makes it easy for skydivers to climb out and jump, so it is a favourite at skydiving centres.
The FBI in the United States has used at least 27 Cessna 182s fitted with cameras and other surveillance equipment.
Air forces in more than a dozen countries have flown the 182.
Production stopped in 1985, restarted in 1996, stopped again in 2012 and restarted in 2015.
spotterTips: It looks a lot like a Cessna 172, with a high strut-braced wing, a nose wheel and one propeller. Look for a slightly bigger, chunkier body, a larger engine cowling and often a constant speed propeller with a pointed spinner.

melbourne.where: Seen at Moorabbin and Lilydale, and at skydiving centres and country airfields across Victoria.
melbourne.operators: Private owners, aero clubs, skydiving operators and aerial survey companies

name: Tecnam P2008
role: Two-seat training and light sport aeroplane
summary: The Tecnam P2008 is a modern two-seat aeroplane from Italy that many flight schools use to train new pilots. It mixes a carbon fibre body with metal wings, which makes it light and efficient.
funFacts: It was the first Tecnam aircraft to use major parts made from carbon fibre.
Its nose wheel is not connected to the rudder pedals. The pilot steers on the ground by braking one main wheel or the other.
The same basic design can be certified in three different categories, including light sport aircraft and the European CS-VLA rules.
It has an all-moving tailplane, so the whole horizontal tail tilts instead of just a hinged flap.
spotterTips: Look for a high wing held up by a single strut on each side, one propeller, a nose wheel and a sleek, rounded carbon fibre body. The horizontal tail is mounted low and moves as one piece.

melbourne.where: Tecnam training aircraft fly from Moorabbin and other Victorian training airfields, so keep an eye out for the P2008 among the Cessnas and Pipers.
melbourne.operators: Flight schools and private owners

photo.artist: Alan Wilson from Stilton, Peterborough, Cambs, UK

name: Diamond DA42 Twin Star
role: Four-seat twin-engine training and touring aeroplane
engines: 2 × Austro Engine AE 300 turbocharged diesel engines (125 kW each)
summary: The DA42 Twin Star is a sleek four-seat aeroplane with two diesel engines that run on jet fuel. It is made mostly from composite materials and is popular with flight schools for teaching pilots how to fly twin-engine aircraft.
funFacts: In 2004 a DA42 became the first diesel-powered aeroplane to fly non-stop across the North Atlantic, using only about 22 litres of fuel per hour.
In 2010 a DA42 became the first aircraft publicly flown on fuel made from algae.
By 2008 it had about 80 per cent of the world market for new piston twin aeroplanes.
A pilotless military surveillance drone called the Dominator was developed from the DA42.
spotterTips: Look for a low wing with a long, slender span, two engines on the wing, a T-tail and a smooth, shiny composite body with a big bubble canopy. The upturned winglets at the wing tips are another clue.

melbourne.where: Some flight schools at Moorabbin Airport use the DA42 for twin-engine training, so watch for it in the circuit there.
melbourne.operators: Flight schools and private owners

name: Beechcraft Bonanza
status: In service, with production ending after the last orders are built
summary: The Bonanza is a fast, comfortable single-engine aeroplane with retractable landing gear that has been built since 1947. It holds the record for the longest continuously produced aircraft in the world, although Textron announced in 2025 that production is ending.
funFacts: No other aircraft in the world has been in continuous production for as long as the Bonanza.
Early Bonanzas had a V-shaped tail with just two tail surfaces instead of the usual three.
In 1949 a Bonanza made the first light aircraft flight from Hawaii to mainland United States, about 4,700 km.
When it first appeared it was all metal with retractable wheels, while many small planes were still made of wood and fabric.
spotterTips: Look for a low wing, one propeller and wheels that fold up after take-off. Older models have a distinctive V-shaped tail, while newer ones like the G36 have a normal tail. The G36 also has double doors at the back for passengers.

melbourne.where: Bonanzas are flown by private owners and visit Moorabbin, Essendon Fields and country airfields around Victoria.
melbourne.operators: Private owners and some charter operators

name: Embraer Phenom 300
summary: The Phenom 300 is a small, fast business jet from Brazil. It has been the world's best-selling light jet for more than ten years in a row, and it can be flown by just one pilot.
funFacts: It was the most delivered business jet in the world in 2013 and has been the best-selling light jet for many years since.
Some Phenom 300s are assembled in a town called Melbourne, but it is in Florida in the United States.
It is certified to be flown by a single pilot, even though it cruises at more than 800 km/h.
It can fly higher than 13,000 metres, well above most airliners' cruising height.
spotterTips: Look for a low swept wing with upturned winglets, a T-tail and two jet engines mounted on the back of the body. It has a smooth, rounded nose and large oval cabin windows.

melbourne.where: Essendon Fields is the best place to see business jets like the Phenom 300, and they also visit Melbourne Airport and Avalon.
melbourne.operators: Charter companies and private owners

name: North American XB-70 Valkyrie
role: Experimental supersonic bomber and research aircraft
status: Retired (one survivor is in a museum)
summary: The XB-70 Valkyrie was a giant white bomber designed to fly at three times the speed of sound. The bomber was cancelled, so only two were built and they were used for high-speed research instead. It still looks like something from science fiction.
funFacts: It could cruise at about Mach 3, roughly 3,200 km/h, for long periods.
The outer parts of its wings could fold down by up to 65 degrees at high speed to help it stay stable and ride on its own shock wave.
The name Valkyrie was chosen from about 20,000 entries in a naming contest in 1958.
The only surviving XB-70 is on display at the National Museum of the United States Air Force in Ohio.
spotterTips: It has a huge delta wing, a long thin nose with small canard wings near the cockpit, twin tail fins and six engines side by side in one giant box under the rear of the body.

name: Virgin Galactic SpaceShipTwo
manufacturer: Scaled Composites and The Spaceship Company, for Virgin Galactic
status: Retired (the last flight was on 8 June 2024)
summary: SpaceShipTwo was a rocket-powered spaceplane that carried tourists to the edge of space. A carrier aircraft lifted it high into the sky, then it dropped away, fired its rocket and shot upwards before gliding back to land on a runway like an aeroplane.
funFacts: It did not take off by itself. A huge twin-body jet called WhiteKnightTwo carried it up and released it in mid-air.
To come back down safely, its tail booms folded upwards like a shuttlecock, a trick called feathering.
On 13 December 2018 it climbed higher than 80 km (50 miles) for the first time, which the US counts as reaching space.
Virgin Galactic founder Richard Branson flew on it in July 2021.
spotterTips: Look for a small white spaceplane with a short wing, two tail booms that end in tall fins, and lots of round windows along the cabin. You would normally see it hanging under the middle of the twin-body WhiteKnightTwo carrier.

photo.file: Virgin Galactic SpaceShipTwo "Unity" rollout 19Feb2016, FAITH hangar, Mojave, California.jpg

name: Pipistrel Velis Electro
numberBuilt: More than 100 (the 100th was delivered in March 2024)
engines: 1 × Pipistrel E-811 electric motor (57.6 kW, about 77 hp)
summary: The Velis Electro is a small two-seat training aeroplane powered by an electric motor and batteries instead of petrol. In 2020 it became the first fully electric aeroplane in the world to be type certified, which means it is approved for normal use such as pilot training.
funFacts: It can fly for about 50 minutes plus a safety reserve, which is just right for a training lesson around the airfield.
Its two battery packs are liquid cooled, a bit like a car engine, and can be recharged from 30 to 100 per cent in about two hours.
It is very quiet, with a maximum noise level of about 60 decibels, roughly as loud as people talking.
In 2020 it set seven world records for electric flight, including flying 839 km in 56 hours by making many short flights and recharging in between.
spotterTips: Look for a high wing with no struts, a nose wheel and fixed landing gear, and a slim two-seat cabin with a big clear canopy. The best clue is that it makes almost no engine noise, and there is no exhaust pipe because the motor is electric.

name: Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider
status: In flight testing and early production
numberBuilt: At least 2 flying test aircraft, with more being built
engines: 2 × Pratt & Whitney turbofans (reported to be the PW9000)
summary: The B-21 Raider is a new American stealth bomber shaped like a giant flying wing. It is designed to be very hard for radar to detect, and it will replace older bombers like the B-1 and B-2. Most of its details are still secret.
funFacts: It is named after the Doolittle Raiders, who flew a famous bombing raid on Japan in 1942.
The first B-21 flew on 10 November 2023, and the second joined flight testing at Edwards Air Force Base in California in September 2025.
It is built at a secretive factory called Plant 42 in Palmdale, California.
Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota will be the first base to get operational B-21s.
spotterTips: It is a flying wing with no tail at all, a bit like a smaller B-2 Spirit. Look for a dark grey shape with a pointed nose and engine intakes hidden on top of the wing.
